payload.prompt: What is the OpenAI Python library?

options.text: An official Python SDK for OpenAI models
options.rationale: Correct. It is the official Python SDK for interacting with OpenAI models and services through code instead of raw HTTP requests.

options.text: An Azure Language SDK for text analyzers
options.error_type: Confuses the OpenAI library with the Azure Language SDK
options.rationale: This names a different Python library. Azure Language uses its own SDK for language detection and PII detection.
options.better_fit: Choose this when building Python code for Azure Language capabilities such as detect_language().

feedback.intrinsic: Your app would be set up for language analysis rather than calls to a deployed OpenAI model.
feedback.instructional: Keep the libraries separate: openai connects Python code to OpenAI models, while Azure Language has a different SDK.

options.text: A file that stores environment values
options.error_type: Confuses an SDK with a .env file
options.rationale: A .env file stores named configuration values. It is not a Python library developers install to make model calls.
options.better_fit: Choose this for a .env file that holds an endpoint, API key, and deployment name.

feedback.intrinsic: You would look for connection code in a configuration file instead of installing the library that provides it.
feedback.instructional: A .env file stores values; the OpenAI Python library provides ready-made Python code for the connection.

options.error_type: Confuses an SDK with a deployment name
options.rationale: A deployment name identifies a deployed model. The library is the Python SDK used to interact with that deployment.
options.better_fit: Choose this when referring to a name such as gpt-demo-model assigned during deployment.

feedback.intrinsic: The app could identify a deployment but would still lack the Python library for sending requests.
feedback.instructional: A deployment name selects a model deployment; the SDK provides the code interface used to call it.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The OpenAI Python library is the official SDK for using OpenAI models and services from Python.

payload.prompt: Which statements describe the OpenAI Python library? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is an official Python SDK
options.rationale: Correct. The library is described as the official Python SDK. SDK means software development kit.

options.text: It lets Python code use OpenAI services
options.rationale: Correct. It lets Python applications interact with OpenAI models and services through code.

options.text: It avoids writing raw HTTP requests
options.rationale: Correct. The SDK provides code for interacting with services instead of using raw HTTP requests.

options.error_type: Confuses the OpenAI library with the Azure Language SDK
options.rationale: detect_language() belongs to the Azure Language Python SDK client. It is not the described OpenAI library call.
options.better_fit: Choose this for an Azure Language client that detects a primary language and confidence score.

feedback.intrinsic: A developer expecting this method from the OpenAI library would be working with the wrong library.
feedback.instructional: Use the OpenAI Python library for deployed model interactions; use the Azure Language SDK for detect_language().

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The official SDK lets Python code work with OpenAI models and services without raw HTTP requests.

payload.prompt: Decide whether this statement is true or false.
payload.statement: The OpenAI Python library lets developers use OpenAI models and services through Python code instead of raw HTTP requests.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The SDK provides ready-made Python code for connecting to OpenAI models and services.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing false would overlook the library's main purpose when building a Python application.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The OpenAI Python library is the official SDK for using OpenAI models and services through Python code rather than raw HTTP requests.

payload.prompt: Complete the command used to install the official OpenAI Python SDK.
payload.explanation: The package name identifies which Python library pip installs. The official library for OpenAI models and services uses the name openai.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Installing the other package would prepare the app for Azure Language features instead of OpenAI model access.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use openai here. azure-ai-textanalytics is the package for the Azure Language Python SDK.

payload.prompt: A customer-feedback analyst is building a Python app to send review prompts to a deployed OpenAI model. Which package should she install?

options.rationale: Correct. The openai package installs the official Python SDK for interacting with deployed OpenAI models.

options.error_type: Confuses OpenAI model access with Azure Language tools
options.rationale: This package is for the Azure Language Python SDK. It supports capabilities such as language detection and PII detection.
options.better_fit: Choose this when the app needs Azure Language features such as detect_language() or recognize_pii_entities().

feedback.intrinsic: The analyst would have a package for specialized language analysis, not the requested deployed-model prompts.
feedback.instructional: For prompts sent to a deployed OpenAI model, install openai. Azure Language uses azure-ai-textanalytics.

options.error_type: Confuses loading configuration with model access
options.rationale: load_dotenv() loads values from a .env file. It does not provide the OpenAI model connection.
options.better_fit: Choose this when loading endpoint, key, and deployment-name values from a .env file.

feedback.intrinsic: The app could load saved values but would not gain the library needed to call the deployed model.
feedback.instructional: Configuration loading and model access have different roles. The OpenAI package supplies the Python SDK for model calls.

options.error_type: Confuses Python environment access with the OpenAI SDK
options.rationale: The os package retrieves environment values with os.getenv(). It is not the OpenAI Python SDK.
options.better_fit: Choose this when code needs to retrieve a named environment value after it is loaded.

feedback.intrinsic: The analyst could retrieve a value by name but could not create the OpenAI connection from this package alone.
feedback.instructional: Use os.getenv() for configuration values and openai for interacting with deployed OpenAI models.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Install openai when Python code needs to send prompts to a deployed OpenAI model.

payload.prompt: Which statements correctly match a code editor and a terminal? Select all that apply.

options.text: A code editor is used to write application code
options.rationale: Correct. A code editor is software used to write application code.
Correct. A terminal is a command-line window where commands can run.

options.text: Visual Studio Code can include a terminal
options.rationale: Correct. A terminal can be built into a code editor such as Visual Studio Code.

options.text: A terminal is the OpenAI Python SDK
options.error_type: Confuses a command window with a Python library
options.rationale: A terminal is a command-line window. The OpenAI Python SDK is a library installed for Python code.
options.better_fit: Choose this for the openai library used in Python applications.

feedback.intrinsic: You would search for library features in a place meant for entering commands.
feedback.instructional: The editor and terminal are workspaces for writing and running code; the SDK is code your application imports.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Write application code in the editor, then use its terminal to run commands.

payload.prompt: Where can you run python app.py from inside Visual Studio Code?

options.rationale: Correct. The terminal is the command-line window inside the editor where Python commands can run.

options.error_type: Confuses a configuration file with a command window
options.rationale: A .env file stores named configuration values. It does not run application commands.
options.better_fit: Choose this for storing values such as an endpoint and API key.

feedback.intrinsic: Putting a run command there would leave the application unstarted.
feedback.instructional: Use the terminal to run python app.py. Use .env only to store configuration values.

options.error_type: Confuses a model identifier with a command window
options.rationale: A deployment name identifies a deployed model. It is not a place where commands are entered.
options.better_fit: Choose this when selecting the model deployment for a request.

feedback.intrinsic: The model could be named correctly, but the application would still not run.
feedback.instructional: A deployment name selects a deployed model; a terminal runs the Python command.

options.error_type: Confuses a Python object with a command window
options.rationale: A client object makes authorized calls from application code. It is not a command-line window.
options.better_fit: Choose this after obtaining an endpoint and API key for calls from Python code.

feedback.intrinsic: The client can be used only after the application is running, so it cannot replace the terminal.
feedback.instructional: Create the client in code, then run that code from the terminal.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The editor's terminal is where you can run python app.py.

payload.prompt: Is the following statement accurate?
payload.statement: A code editor's terminal is where you write the application's Python code.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Write Python code in the editor and use the terminal to run commands.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would mix up the place for writing code with the place for running it.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A code editor is for writing application code. Its terminal is a command-line window for commands such as python <file_name>.py.

payload.prompt: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.
payload.explanation: The sentence first identifies the terminal, then explains where it can appear, what it is, and why it is used. This follows the relationship between a code editor and its built-in command-line window.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The meaning becomes unclear when the location, definition, and purpose are placed out of sequence.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Begin with the terminal, then say it can be inside the editor, define it as a command-line window, and state that it runs commands.

payload.prompt: A developer has finished analyze.py for customer reviews in Visual Studio Code and must test it. Which actions should the developer take? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Visual Studio Code can include a terminal for running commands.
Correct. Running python <file_name>.py in the terminal runs the application.

options.text: Write the command in the .env file
options.error_type: Confuses configuration storage with command execution
options.rationale: A .env file stores named configuration values. It is not where application commands run.
options.better_fit: Choose this when saving values such as API_KEY for the application to load.

feedback.intrinsic: The testing command would be stored as text, so the review analysis would not begin.
feedback.instructional: Open the terminal and enter the Python command there. Keep .env for configuration values.

options.text: Use the deployment name as a command window
options.error_type: Confuses a model identifier with a terminal
options.rationale: A deployment name identifies the model used by a request. A terminal is the command-line window that runs the application.
options.better_fit: Choose this when supplying the deployed model name to the model argument.

feedback.intrinsic: The app would have no command-line window in which to start its review analysis.
feedback.instructional: Use the terminal to run analyze.py; use a deployment name inside the code to select the deployed model.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. After writing analyze.py, open the terminal and run python analyze.py to test it.

payload.prompt: What does a .env file store?

options.rationale: Correct. A .env file stores named configuration values such as an endpoint, API key, and deployment name.

options.error_type: Confuses configuration with model output
options.rationale: Generated output is returned after a model request. A .env file holds configuration values used by the application.
options.better_fit: Choose this when referring to output returned from client.responses.create().

feedback.intrinsic: Saving a response as configuration would not provide the endpoint, key, and deployment details needed for later calls.
feedback.instructional: A .env file stores setup values. Generated output is the result of a request, not configuration.

options.error_type: Confuses configuration with a model deployment
options.rationale: A deployed model is accessed through a Foundry resource. A .env file can store its deployment name, not the model itself.
options.better_fit: Choose this when referring to the model that has been deployed in Foundry.

feedback.intrinsic: The application would still need access to the deployed model outside its local configuration file.
feedback.instructional: Store the deployment name in .env so code can select the deployed model when making a request.

options.error_type: Confuses stored values with a Python object
options.rationale: The OpenAI client object is created in Python from an endpoint and API key. A .env file stores those values for the code to load.
options.better_fit: Choose this for the authenticated object created with base_url and api_key.

feedback.intrinsic: The app would lack the configured object that actually makes authorized calls.
feedback.instructional: The .env file supplies values; Python code uses those values to create the client object.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. A .env file stores named configuration values, including endpoint, key, and deployment name.

payload.prompt: Which values can be environment variables in a .env file? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. An endpoint is a named configuration value that can be stored in .env.
Correct. An API key is a named configuration value stored in the shown .env files.
Correct. MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME stores the name used to call a deployed model.

options.text: A sentence generated by the model
options.error_type: Confuses configuration values with model output
options.rationale: A generated sentence is request output. Environment variables are named values used to configure the application.
options.better_fit: Choose this for output returned after a request to the deployed model.

feedback.intrinsic: The application would save a result where it needs a reusable connection or deployment value.
feedback.instructional: Keep endpoints, keys, and deployment names in .env. Generated wording belongs to the response from a request.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Endpoints, API keys, and deployment names are named configuration values suitable for .env.

payload.prompt: Evaluate this statement.
payload.statement: A key in a .env file must exactly match the name requested by os.getenv() in code.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Exact matching lets os.getenv() retrieve the intended value.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A mismatch leaves the application unable to retrieve the configuration value it expects.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: If code requests API_KEY, the .env file must use API_KEY exactly. Consistent names avoid missing values at runtime.

payload.prompt: Complete the Python function that reads a named environment value.
payload.explanation: load_dotenv() loads stored .env values into the application environment, while os.getenv() retrieves one value by its name. The endpoint assignment needs the retrieval step.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Using a loading call or a response call here would not place the named endpoint value into endpoint.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use getenv to retrieve AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT. load_dotenv() has the earlier job of loading .env values, and responses.create() sends a model request.

payload.prompt: A developer's customer-review app cannot find its API key. The .env file says APIKEY, but the code calls os.getenv("API_KEY"). What should the developer change?

options.rationale: Correct. The .env key must exactly match the name requested by os.getenv() in code.

options.text: Replace the key with a deployment name
options.error_type: Confuses an API key variable with a deployment name
options.rationale: A deployment name selects a deployed model. It cannot replace the API key used to authorize access.
options.better_fit: Choose a deployment name when setting MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME for the model argument.

feedback.intrinsic: The app would still have no matching API key value for authorization.
feedback.instructional: Keep each configuration value in its own role: API_KEY authorizes access, while a deployment name selects the model.

options.text: Put the API key in the model output
options.error_type: Confuses configuration with generated output
options.rationale: The API key is configuration used to create an authenticated client. Model output is returned after a request.
options.better_fit: Choose model output when referring to results returned from a deployed model request.

feedback.intrinsic: The app could not use a returned response to fix the missing configuration before making its call.
feedback.instructional: Store the API key in .env under the exact name the code requests.

options.error_type: Confuses loading configuration with variable naming
options.rationale: load_dotenv() loads .env values into the application environment. Removing it does not fix the mismatch between APIKEY and API_KEY.
options.better_fit: Choose this only when discussing whether an application loads values from a .env file.

feedback.intrinsic: The app would have even less access to the saved configuration values.
feedback.instructional: Keep load_dotenv() and make the .env key match os.getenv("API_KEY") exactly.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Rename the .env key to API_KEY so the saved name exactly matches the name requested in code.

payload.prompt: Which statements about a model deployment name are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is assigned when a model is deployed
options.rationale: Correct. A deployment name is assigned to a model when it is deployed.
Correct. gpt-demo-model is a stated example of a customized deployment name.

options.text: It can match the model name if unchanged
options.rationale: Correct. When the name is not customized, it can match a model name such as gpt-4.1-mini.

options.text: It is the API key used for authorization
options.error_type: Confuses a deployment name with an API key
options.rationale: An API key proves authorization. A deployment name identifies which deployed model receives the request.
options.better_fit: Choose this for API_KEY, which is used when creating an authenticated client.

feedback.intrinsic: The application might select a name but would not have the authorization value needed to connect.
feedback.instructional: Use the deployment name as the model value and the API key to authorize access.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. A deployment name is assigned during deployment and may be customized or left to match the model name.

payload.prompt: Is the following statement accurate?
payload.statement: A model deployment name is always different from the model name.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. A customized deployment can differ, but an unchanged name can match the model name.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Treating the names as always different could make a developer overlook the deployment name actually in use.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A model may be given a custom deployment name such as gpt-demo-model. If it is not customized, the deployment name can match gpt-4.1-mini.

payload.prompt: Put the pieces in the correct order.
payload.explanation: The order defines the term before stating when it is assigned. It clearly connects the name to the model deployment event.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A mixed order can make it unclear whether the name belongs to the model or to another configuration value.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with the term, define it as a name, then connect it to the model and its deployment.

payload.prompt: Complete the configuration variable for the name used to call a deployed model.
payload.explanation: The application retrieves MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME and passes that value as the model when making a request. An API key authorizes access, while an endpoint identifies the service address.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Using the key or endpoint variable here would leave the application without the name needed to select the deployed model.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME for gpt-4.1-mini. API_KEY and AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT have different configuration roles.

payload.prompt: A bank deploys gpt-4.1 to summarize loan applications and names the deployment support-reviewer. Which choices should its app use to select that deployment? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. support-reviewer is the assigned deployment name, so it identifies the deployed model.
Correct. This configuration variable can store the name assigned to the deployed model.
Correct. client.responses.create() uses model=deployment_name to send a request to a specific deployment.

options.text: The API key as the model argument
options.error_type: Confuses authorization with model selection
options.rationale: The API key proves authorization when creating the client. It does not identify the deployed model in the model argument.
options.better_fit: Choose this when setting api_key while creating the OpenAI client object.

feedback.intrinsic: The bank's request would not identify support-reviewer as the model deployment to use.
feedback.instructional: Pass the deployment name to model. Use the API key separately to authorize the client connection.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Store support-reviewer as MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME and pass that value to the model argument.

payload.prompt: What does an authenticated OpenAI client object enable?

options.text: Authorized API calls to a service
options.rationale: Correct. A configured client object can securely make authorized API calls without code manually managing tokens or secrets.

options.text: Language detection without a service call
options.error_type: Confuses the OpenAI client with Azure Language analysis
options.rationale: Language detection is an Azure Language capability called through its client. The OpenAI client makes authorized calls to a deployed model.
options.better_fit: Choose this for Azure Language language detection through TextAnalyticsClient.

feedback.intrinsic: The application would not obtain a language result merely by creating an OpenAI client.
feedback.instructional: An OpenAI client connects to a deployed model. Language detection uses the Azure Language client and its detect_language() method.

options.error_type: Confuses a client object with a .env file
options.rationale: A .env file stores endpoint, key, and deployment-name values. The client object is created from loaded endpoint and key values.
options.better_fit: Choose this for the .env file used to save named configuration values.

feedback.intrinsic: The application would have stored values but no authenticated object for making the call.
feedback.instructional: Load configuration from .env, then use the endpoint and API key to create the OpenAI client.

options.error_type: Confuses a client object with a deployment identifier
options.rationale: A deployment name selects a model. A client object is the configured connection that sends authorized requests.
options.better_fit: Choose this for MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME, which identifies a deployed model.

feedback.intrinsic: A name alone would not create the authorized connection needed to send the request.
feedback.instructional: Use both pieces correctly: the client authorizes and connects, while the deployment name selects the model.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The authenticated client object enables authorized API calls without manually managing tokens or secrets.

payload.prompt: Decide whether this statement is true or false.
payload.statement: An OpenAI client object can be created with a base URL and API key.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The base URL and API key configure the client for an authorized connection.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing false would prevent the developer from using the shown connection details to create the client.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The OpenAI client is created with base_url set to the endpoint and api_key set to the API key.

payload.prompt: Complete the SDK call that creates a response from a deployed model.
payload.explanation: The configured OpenAI client uses responses.create() to send a prompt to the named deployment. The rejected methods belong to the Azure Language client for language and PII analysis.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Using an Azure Language method on this client would not send the prompt to the deployed OpenAI model.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use client.responses.create() here. detect_language() and recognize_pii_entities() are called through TextAnalyticsClient.

payload.prompt: A legal-document team needs its Python app to send case-file summaries to a deployed OpenAI model. It has an endpoint and API key. What should the developer create next?

options.rationale: Correct. The endpoint and API key are used as base_url and api_key to create the authenticated OpenAI client.

options.error_type: Confuses the OpenAI client with the Azure Language client
options.rationale: TextAnalyticsClient is for Azure Language features such as language detection and PII detection. The team needs to send prompts to a deployed OpenAI model.
options.better_fit: Choose this when the legal team needs Azure Language functions such as recognize_pii_entities().

feedback.intrinsic: The team would create a client for specialized language analysis rather than the requested case-summary prompts.
feedback.instructional: For a deployed OpenAI model, create OpenAI(base_url=endpoint, api_key=api_key).

options.error_type: Confuses model selection with an authenticated client
options.rationale: A deployment name is needed to select the model in a request. It does not itself create the authorized connection.
options.better_fit: Choose this when setting the model value in client.responses.create().

feedback.intrinsic: The team could name a model but could not send its case-file prompt without a configured client.
feedback.instructional: Create the OpenAI client from endpoint and key, then use the deployment name in the request.

options.error_type: Confuses stored configuration with a service client
options.rationale: A .env file stores configuration values for code to load. The endpoint and API key must then be used to create a client object.
options.better_fit: Choose this when the team needs to store endpoint, API key, and deployment name values.

feedback.intrinsic: The values could be saved, but the app would still have no object to make the authorized call.
feedback.instructional: A .env file is storage for configuration. The next connection step is creating the OpenAI client object.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Create an OpenAI client object with the endpoint as base_url and the API key for authorization.

payload.prompt: Which statements describe probabilistic model output? Select all that apply.

options.text: Equivalent prompts can vary across calls
options.rationale: Correct. Equivalent prompts can produce different results across calls because generated output is probabilistic.
Correct. Slight differences in wording are a stated form of variation.
Correct. Formatting can also vary slightly between calls.

options.error_type: Confuses probabilistic generation with deterministic output
options.rationale: Deterministic results stay consistent for a specific task. Generative-model output can vary in wording or formatting between equivalent prompts.
options.better_fit: Choose this when referring to Azure Language analyzers that return structured, deterministic results.

feedback.intrinsic: A workflow expecting an identical format every time could receive slightly different generated wording instead.
feedback.instructional: Probabilistic means variation is possible. Choose Azure Language when consistent structured values are required.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Probabilistic generation means equivalent prompts can return slightly different wording or formatting.

payload.prompt: Is the following statement accurate?
payload.statement: The same prompt always returns exactly the same wording and formatting from a generative model.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Generated output can vary slightly in wording or formatting between calls.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Expecting an exact repeat could make an automated workflow depend on formatting that changes on a later call.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Generative-model output is probabilistic, so equivalent prompts can return slightly different wording or formatting.

payload.prompt: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.
payload.explanation: The sequence states what can vary, then describes the variation and the condition under which it occurs. It captures why equivalent prompts are not guaranteed to have identical generated results.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A scrambled order can hide the important link between variation and equivalent prompts.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with generative output, state that it can vary, then say the variation happens between calls for equivalent prompts.

payload.prompt: Complete the term: output that can vary between equivalent prompts is ____.

parts.text: Generated model output can vary in wording or formatting between equivalent calls because it is

payload.explanation: Probabilistic generation allows slight variation in wording or formatting across calls. Deterministic output is the contrasting choice used when consistent structured values matter.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Calling the output deterministic would create the wrong expectation of identical results for equivalent prompts.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use probabilistic because generated wording or formatting can vary. Deterministic describes the consistent structured results provided by Azure Language analyzers.

payload.prompt: A healthcare system must return a language code, confidence score, and redacted patient text in consistent structured values. Which choices fit this need? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Azure Language is the better choice when language codes, confidence scores, or redacted text must be consistent structured values.
Correct. Purpose-built language analyzers return structured, deterministic results for specific tasks.
Correct. Deterministic structured output fits an application that needs consistent values.

options.error_type: Confuses flexible generative output with predictable structured analysis
options.rationale: Generated wording can vary between calls. The required codes, scores, and redacted text call for consistent structured results.
options.better_fit: Choose this for flexible conversational analysis where a fixed structured output is not required.

feedback.intrinsic: Patient-processing results could vary in wording or formatting when the workflow needs consistent fields.
feedback.instructional: For language codes, confidence scores, and redacted text, use Azure Language and its deterministic structured results.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Azure Language purpose-built analyzers return the consistent structured values this healthcare workflow needs.

payload.prompt: A support-team manager must route every incoming ticket by an exact language code and confidence score. Which reasons support choosing Azure Language instead of a general-purpose model? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Azure Language analyzers return structured, deterministic output for specific tasks.

options.text: It is better for language codes and confidence scores
options.rationale: Correct. Language detection returns a primary language, ISO 639-1 code, and confidence score, which are consistent structured values.

options.text: Generative output can vary between calls
options.rationale: Correct. General-purpose model output is probabilistic, so equivalent prompts can vary in wording or formatting.

options.text: A general-purpose model has no language ability
options.error_type: Confuses output predictability with language capability
options.rationale: General-purpose models have broad language understanding and can perform many text-analysis tasks. The reason to choose Azure Language here is predictable structured output, not an absence of language ability.
options.better_fit: Choose this for no stated situation; general-purpose models do have broad language capabilities.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager could reject useful general-purpose analysis for the wrong reason instead of choosing based on the routing requirement.
feedback.instructional: Both approaches handle language. Azure Language is the better fit here because exact codes and confidence scores need consistent structured results.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Azure Language fits ticket routing because it returns consistent structured language results, while generated output can vary.

flashcards.front: What is the OpenAI Python library?
flashcards.back: The official Python SDK for OpenAI models and services.
It runs command-line commands, including Python applications.
flashcards.hint: It can be built into a code editor.

flashcards.back: It retrieves an environment value by its exact name.

flashcards.front: Why choose Azure Language for structured values?
flashcards.hint: Use it for codes, scores, or redacted text.
